conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the health claim is true and provides clinical evidence and guidelines from the WHO supporting the conclusion that tenofovir started in the third trimester reduces mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
### Conclusion
The health claim is **true**. Clinical evidence and major global health guidance establish that initiating tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) in the third trimester for pregnant women with chronic hepatitis B (HBV) and high viral loads significantly reduces mother-to-child transmission (MTCT).

### Evidence

1. **Demonstrated Reduction in Transmission:** In a major clinical trial, daily tenofovir treatment starting in the third trimester reduced the HBV MTCT rate from 18% in the control group to 5% in the treated group among mothers with high viral loads ([NYU Langone](https://nyulangone.org/news/antiviral-treatment-during-pregnancy-reduces-mother-child-transmission-hepatitis-b)).
2. **Global Guidelines:** The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends tenofovir prophylaxis for pregnant women with high HBV viral loads (HBV DNA ≥ 5.3 log10 IU/mL) to prevent MTCT alongside standard infant immunoprophylaxis ([WHO Guidelines](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/978-92-4-000270-8)).
3. **Origin of Skepticism:** Doubt regarding this claim often stems from individual studies (such as Jourdain et al.) where transmission rates were low in both control and treatment groups (e.g., 0/147 vs. 3/147) because infants already received prompt hepatitis B vaccination and immune globulin at birth, resulting in small numerical differences that did not reach statistical significance in single trials ([Irish Medical Journal](https://imj.ie/prevention-of-mother-to-child-transmission-in-patients-with-chronic-hepatitis-b-virus-infection-and-high-viral-loads/)). 

However, broader evidence syntheses and systematic reviews confirm that peripartum tenofovir prophylaxis provides critical added protection against vertical transmission ([The Lancet Infectious Diseases](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(20)30586-7/abstract)).
